newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Russia says ready to negotiate ties with NATO.
newsitem.headline: Russia says ready to negotiate ties with NATO.

text.p: Russia signalled on Tuesday it was ready to put aside its arguments over NATO's planned expansion and start talks on a charter governing all aspects of the relationship with the 16-nation alliance.

A NATO official said Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov had asked when Moscow could start the dialogue during a meeting with NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana despite the alliance's decision to press ahead with eastwards expansion.

Hours before Primakov arrived in Brussels for his talks with Solana and NATO foreign ministers, Moscow reiterated its opposition to the alliance's plans for enlargement, which it says threatens Russia's security.
But Moscow's protests seemed to be becoming less tenable in the face of NATO's point-blank refusal to scrap its plans for admitting east European states which were once Kremlin allies.

"It is interesting that they (the Russians) are now indicating a willingness to talk to us on the essentials. They are no longer asking us to change the enlargement policy before they can talk," said the NATO official.

He said Primakov had not referred to enlargement during his brief 20-minute meeting with Solana. The Russian, who also met U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher, is due to meet NATO foreign ministers for further substantive talks on Wednesday.
The alliance devised the idea of a charter with Russia in a bid to reassure Moscow it had no aggressive intentions.

Defence officials say one possibility would be to form a new structure which might give Moscow a say in running the alliance. Russian contacts with NATO currently fall under the alliance's "16 plus one" structure, a body set up to hold talks between NATO and other countries.
"It is a little bit early to say what the method of consulation with Russia will be. We want to open a debate on this with our Russian friends," Solana told a news conference.
"May be on some issues it we could go a bit farther than 16 plus one," he added.
In another bid to calm tensions with Moscow, Christopher on Tuesday declared the alliance had no plans to station nuclear missiles on the territory of new members.
Russian officials have been united in fierce opposition to NATO's enlargement plans in recent weeks after several months of waveirng between tough rejections and signs of compromise.
Earlier on Tuesday Russian President Boris Yeltsin's press aide dismissed as "fantasy" suggestions Moscow was ready to accept NATO's eastward expansion plans.

Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin voiced Russia's fears at a summit of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) in Lisbon last week, but most other leaders at the meeting backed NATO's plans.
During their talks on Tuesday NATO foreign ministers fixed a date for a summit next year to identify potential new members.
